title: Joshua 1:10–18
context: Joshua turns at once from receiving the LORD’s word to commanding the officers of the people: they are to prepare food, because within three days Israel is to cross the Jordan and possess the land the LORD their God gives them. He then reminds the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh of Moses’ word. Their households may remain in the land already granted east of the Jordan, but their warriors must cross armed and help their brothers until the LORD has given those brothers rest and possession; then they may return to their own inheritance toward the sunrise. They pledge to do all Joshua commands and to go wherever he sends them, asking that the LORD be with him as he was with Moses, and they themselves repeat the charge, “Only be strong and courageous.” Both traditions read the scene as Israel receiving Joshua’s leadership under the same LORD who was with Moses, and as the eastern tribes honoring their earlier word. The land remains the LORD’s gift.

verses.text: Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Joshua commands the officers of the people. He does not delay after the LORD’s speech; he turns at once to orderly preparation through the leaders already set over the camp.

Arminian readers hear obedient action. The word received in verses 1–9 now becomes a word Joshua actually gives; he exercises real responsibility under God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Joshua’s first public act is to command what the LORD has already required. The officers are drawn into the same commission; leadership here is the mediation of God’s word, not a new plan of Joshua’s own.

Both traditions take the verse as Joshua beginning to carry out the charge, on shared ground.

verses.text: “Pass through the middle of the camp, and command the people, saying, ‘Prepare food; for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan, to go in to possess the land which the LORD your God gives you to possess.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The officers are to pass through the camp and tell the people, “Prepare food; for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan, to go in to possess the land which the LORD your God gives you to possess.”

Arminian readers hear a near, practical obedience: food, three days, and a crossing they must actually make. The land is what God gives, and they are to go in and possess it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the giver: the LORD their God gives them the land to possess. The three days set a real near term for the crossing, and the command assumes the promise already spoken.

How the “three days” lines up with the spy mission of chapter 2 and the later crossing is a narrative timing question readers discuss; both traditions take the command itself as Joshua’s faithful response to the LORD.

verses.text: Joshua spoke to the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to the half-tribe of Manasseh, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua speaks to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, the tribes already granted land east of the Jordan. He does not leave their earlier agreement with Moses unspoken.

Arminian readers hear a pointed, personal address. These tribes have received their rest in one sense, and they are still called to keep their word to their brothers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Joshua takes up Moses’ arrangement rather than inventing a new policy for the eastern tribes. Continuity with the servant of the LORD marks his leadership.

Both traditions take the verse as the start of a reminder about covenant solidarity, shared ground for the charge that follows.

verses.text: “Remember the word which Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, ‘The LORD your God gives you rest, and will give you this land.
verses.arminianNotes:
They are to remember the word Moses the servant of the LORD commanded them: “The LORD your God gives you rest, and will give you this land.” Rest and the land are named as the LORD’s gifts, already spoken through Moses.

Arminian readers hear a call to memory that obliges them. The rest they have been given is meant to issue in faithful help, not in early withdrawal from the people’s work.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that rest is what God gives. The land east of the Jordan is already framed as the LORD’s gift, and Joshua only recalls the word Moses commanded.

Both traditions take “rest” here as the LORD’s gift of a settled inheritance, a theme later Scripture will also take up, without forcing a later debate back into this verse.

verses.text: Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall live in the land which Moses gave you beyond the Jordan; but you shall pass over before your brothers armed, all the mighty men of valor, and shall help them
verses.arminianNotes:
Their wives, little ones, and livestock may remain in the land Moses gave them beyond the Jordan, but the mighty men of valor are to pass over armed before their brothers and help them.

Arminian readers hear a costly, concrete duty. Possession of their own land does not cancel responsibility; they must actually go first and help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the eastern grant as already given by Moses, and the armed crossing as the obligation that accompanied that grant. Help for the brothers is part of the same word, not an extra courtesy.

Both traditions take the verse as covenant solidarity: their rest does not excuse them from their brothers’ need.

verses.text: until the LORD has given your brothers rest, as he has given you, and they have also possessed the land which the LORD your God gives them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and possess it, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
They are to remain until the LORD has given their brothers rest, as he has given them, and until those brothers have also possessed the land the LORD their God gives them. Then they may return to their own possession toward the sunrise.

Arminian readers hear a clear term and a real return. The duty has an end, and it is set by what God does for the others, not by the eastern tribes’ impatience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the repeated giver: the LORD gives rest and the land to the brothers, as he has already given to these tribes. Their return is allowed only after that gift is in place.

Both traditions read the arrangement as temporary, purposeful, and grounded in the LORD’s gift to the whole people.

verses.text: They answered Joshua, saying, “All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.
verses.arminianNotes:
They answer Joshua, “All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.” The reply, in context, comes from the tribes just addressed.

Arminian readers hear a real pledge of obedience and availability. They bind themselves to do and to go, words that will have to be kept in the campaigns ahead.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same pledge as the right reception of Joshua’s authority, in line with the word Moses had already laid on them. Their yes is a submission to the LORD’s appointed leader.

Both traditions take the answer as a sincere commitment. The immediate speakers are the eastern tribes, though the wording models loyalty to Joshua.

verses.text: Just as we listened to Moses in all things, so will we listen to you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Just as we listened to Moses in all things, so will we listen to you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses.”

Arminian readers hear loyalty joined to a prayer. They will listen as they listened to Moses, and they ask for the presence that alone can make Joshua’s leadership hold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the “Only”: Joshua’s place like Moses’ depends on the LORD being with him, which is exactly what God has already promised in verse 5. The people ask for what God has pledged.

Both traditions take the verse as recognition that Joshua’s authority stands with God’s presence, not in mere succession to Moses’ name.

verses.text: Whoever rebels against your commandment, and doesn’t listen to your words in all that you command him shall himself be put to death. Only be strong and courageous.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Whoever rebels against Joshua’s commandment and does not listen to his words in all that he commands is to be put to death. They close with, “Only be strong and courageous.”

Arminian readers hear how seriously they take the new leader’s word, and they hear the tribes themselves now repeating the LORD’s charge to Joshua. Courage is urged by the people as well as by God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the death sanction as the community’s own pledge to suppress rebellion against the appointed commander, and they hear “Only be strong and courageous” as an echo of the LORD’s repeated word in verses 6–9.

Both traditions take the closing charge as shared ground with the opening commission, not as a different call to self-reliance.
